question: What does the spread of healthcare improvement primarily involve?

options.A: Reducing the number of staff working in a ward
options.B: Purchasing expensive equipment for a single department
options.C: Scaling a successful local project across multiple units
options.D: Writing a new hospital policy without testing it

explanation: Spread means taking a proven local pilot and implementing it across other departments or facilities to benefit more patients. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do many useful clinical innovations fail to spread across a hospital?

options.A: Government policies strictly ban inter-ward cooperation
options.B: Lack of a deliberate strategy for wider adoption
options.C: Doctors prefer working with outdated medical equipment
options.D: Patients refuse to accept new nursing care methods

explanation: Without an intentional plan to share and scale successful practices, they remain isolated within their original units. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which factor is a major barrier when scaling quality improvement projects?

options.A: Resistance to change among healthcare staff
options.B: Patients demanding new care protocols daily
options.D: Too many nurses trained in quality control

explanation: Staff frequently stick to old habits, making it difficult to introduce new care procedures across units. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h2)

question: How do resource constraints negatively affect the spread of improvement?

options.A: They limit the materials and staffing needed for expansion
options.B: They automatically improve patient recovery rates overnight
options.C: They force management to close down all hospital wards
options.D: They increase the salary of every nurse in the facility

explanation: Scaling requires resources like time, staff, and supplies; shortages make broader implementation nearly impossible. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the role of a local champion in quality improvement?

options.A: Purchasing medical supplies from international vendors
options.B: Punishing staff who refuse to follow new rules
options.C: Advocating for the new practice among peers
options.D: Writing hospital budgets for the upcoming fiscal year

explanation: Local champions use their influence to encourage other staff members to embrace and sustain the new changes. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why should an improvement project be adapted before entering a new unit?

options.A: To fit the specific workflow and culture of that unit
options.B: To hide the original results from the hospital management
options.C: To ensure the nursing staff stop using documentation charts
options.D: To make the project much harder for nurses to complete

explanation: Every unit has unique dynamics, so customizing the approach ensures it integrates smoothly into daily routines. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is a recommended first step when preparing to spread an innovation?

options.A: Fire all unit managers who disagree with the project
options.B: Package the improvement into clear, teachable toolkits
options.C: Stop collecting data on patient outcomes immediately
options.D: Keep all implementation details secret from other wards

explanation: Clear toolkits make it easy for other departments to understand and replicate the successful practice. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why are regular feedback loops important during the spread of an initiative?

options.A: To track progress and address emerging problems quickly
options.B: To delay the project until funding runs out completely
options.C: To replace the need for direct patient bedside care
options.D: To give nurses extra paperwork to fill out every shift

explanation: Feedback loops provide real-time data so teams can fix challenges before they derail the entire improvement effort. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h4)

question: How is sustainability of an improvement best achieved in a healthcare facility?

options.A: Waiting for patients to demand better clinical services
options.B: Relying solely on verbal reminders during shift handovers
options.C: Embedding the practice into standard operating procedures
options.D: Stopping all data collection once the project is launched

explanation: Incorporating new methods into official policies and training manuals ensures they outlast initial enthusiasm. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the main danger when leadership support fades after an improvement is spread?

options.A: Nurses refuse to document any clinical procedures
options.B: Patient admission rates drop to zero across all wards
options.C: Staff often slip back into old, familiar habits
options.D: The hospital automatically receives increased government funding

explanation: Without ongoing leadership reinforcement, people naturally revert to older, easier routines over time. [learn more](GST319_U1_T6#GST319_U1_T6_h5)
